Francisco Madero. The Mexican politician and revolutionary who challenged Porfirio Díaz's dictatorship in 1910 and briefly served as president during the early Mexican Revolution. His moderate reformism and inability to satisfy radical factions made his presidency turbulent and brief.

Madero published The Presidential Succession of 1910, a book advocating for free elections and challenging Díaz's reelection. These ideas triggered the Mexican Revolution. His slogan "No reelection" resonated across Mexico and mobilised peasants, workers, and intellectuals against the Porfiriato. He forced Porfirio Díaz to resign in May 1911 and was elected president. However, his moderate land reforms deeply disappointed radical agrarians like Emiliano Zapata. When Madero rejected the radical Plan de Ayala, he alienated southern revolutionaries and created a dangerous schism within the revolution itself. In 1913, he was overthrown in a military coup by Victoriano Huerta. While under army guard, he was killed alongside his vice president. His murder reignited the revolution and shifted it toward greater social radicalism. The moderate vision Madero had championed gave way to the more radical agrarianism and social transformation that would define the revolution's legacy.
